items.s: Imagine ____ at your desk all day with almost nothing to do.

tfn.s: A short quiet period at work is the same as rust-out.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "Rust-out is different because the feeling continues for weeks or months and starts to affect how someone thinks about themselves."

tfn.s: The American Psychological Association wrote about this problem in September 2026.
tfn.why: The text says: "The American Psychological Association discussed this problem in a September 2026 article."

tfn.s: Rust-out is more common in offices than in factories.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not compare rust-out in offices and factories.

tfn.s: Rust-out can happen when work is too easy or repetitive.
tfn.why: The text says: "But psychologists also talk about rust-out, which can happen when work is too easy, too repetitive or has little meaning."

tfn.s: The text says managers can do nothing to help.
tfn.why: The text says managers "can also look at how jobs are organised and give people more freedom".

focus.note: Some verbs go naturally with certain nouns. Think about which verb you usually hear with each word.

tfn.s: Financial commitments can make leaving a job impossible.
tfn.why: The text says: "Financial commitments can make leaving impossible."

tfn.s: Reducing an employee's workload always makes work healthier.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "Simply reducing an employee's workload does not necessarily make their working life healthier."

tfn.s: Rust-out affects more workers than burnout.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say how many workers rust-out affects compared with burnout.

tfn.s: Rust-out differs from burnout in its cause.
tfn.why: The text says: "Unlike burnout, which is associated with excessive workplace stress, rust-out involves chronic boredom, insufficient challenge and a lack of purpose."

tfn.s: The text says that 'I'm bored' sounds more positive to a manager than 'I need a more demanding role'.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: the second sentence "sounds positive", while "I'm bored" may sound like an insult.

focus.note: Many collocations join a verb to a noun, or an adjective to a noun. Decide which word sounds natural before you check the rest of the box.

tfn.s: The writer implies that extra tasks may not help if they are as dull as the existing ones.
tfn.why: The text says: "If the additional work is equally monotonous, it may increase activity without restoring engagement."

tfn.s: The writer says rust-out receives less attention than burnout because its symptoms are physically obvious.
tfn.why: The text says its symptoms "can appear morally uncomfortable", not physically obvious.

tfn.s: The American Psychological Association recommends hiring more staff to reduce boredom.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text gives no recommendation from the association about hiring.

tfn.s: Part of the reason an employee in this position may stay silent is the pressure that other colleagues are under.
tfn.why: The text says such an employee "may hesitate to complain in the presence of colleagues facing intense pressure".

tfn.s: The writer argues that a manager's best first step is to organise a team-building afternoon.
tfn.why: The text suggests asking staff which responsibilities they would welcome, "rather than assuming that another team-building afternoon" will help.

focus.note: Pick the verb that normally partners the noun. These pairs are fixed, so a near synonym often sounds wrong.

items.s: Poorly designed jobs can ____ morale across an entire department.

speak.title: Role-play: a talk about a boring job
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: Your employee looks tired and bored. Find out what is wrong. The team is short of staff, so you cannot give them a new role this month. Offer something smaller, or say no politely.

b.text: Your job is too easy and you feel tired every day. Ask your manager for more interesting work and more freedom to choose your tasks. Explain why it matters to you.

phrases: I'd like to talk about my tasks.
I'm finding the work a bit too easy.
That's not something I expected to hear.
We're short of staff right now, so I can't promise anything.
Could I take on a small project?
Let's try it for a month and see.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did the manager agree to change anything, and was it a fair deal?
